plain.headline: God Looks for Fruit
plain.intro: Today two vineyard stories sit side by side. In Isaiah, God plants a vineyard with great care and it gives only sour grapes. In the Gospel, Jesus retells the story with tenants who refuse the owner his harvest and kill his son. Between them, Paul tells us what good fruit looks like in a life: prayer, peace, and a mind set on what is good.
plain.listen: the owner who keeps sending, and finally sends his son

Reading 1.box: Isaiah sings a love song about a friend who plants a perfect vineyard, only to harvest wild, sour grapes. Then the song turns: the vineyard is God's people, and the fruit God wanted was justice and right living. Isaiah preached in Jerusalem about 700 years before Christ.

chunks.text: Let me sing a song for my dear friend about his vineyard. My friend had a vineyard on a rich hillside. He dug the ground, cleared out the stones, and planted the best vines. He built a watchtower in the middle and carved out a wine press. He expected good grapes, but it gave only wild grapes.
"Now, people of Jerusalem and Judah, you be the judge between me and my vineyard. What more could I have done for it that I did not do? I expected good grapes. Why did it give wild ones?

Here is what I will do to my vineyard. I will pull up its hedge, and animals will eat it. I will knock down its wall, and it will be trampled. I will leave it to ruin. No one will prune it or weed it. Thorns and briers will take over. I will tell the clouds not to rain on it."

The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the people of Israel. The people of Judah are the vines he loved. He looked for justice, but found people being crushed. He looked for right living, but heard cries for help.

Responsorial Psalm.box: The psalm remembers how God brought his people out of Egypt like a vine and planted them in their land. Now the vine lies broken, and the people beg God to look down, care for it again, and give them new life.

Reading 2.box: Paul tells the Christians of Philippi not to worry, but to bring every need to God in prayer, with thanks. God's peace will then guard their hearts. Paul wrote this letter while he was a prisoner, to a church he had founded and loved.

chunks.text: Do not worry about anything. Instead, in every situation, pray and ask God for what you need, and thank him as you do. Then God's peace, which is greater than anything we can understand, will guard your hearts and minds in Christ Jesus.

Finally, my brothers and sisters, fill your minds with whatever is true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, and well spoken of. Whatever is good and worth praising, think about these things. Keep doing what you learned and received from me, what you heard me say and saw me do. Then the God of peace will be with you.

Gospel.box: Jesus tells this parable in the Temple in Jerusalem, a few days before his death, to the chief priests and elders. The owner is God, the servants are the prophets, and the son is Jesus himself. The rejected stone that becomes the cornerstone comes from Psalm 118 and points to his death and resurrection.

chunks.text: "Listen to another parable. A landowner planted a vineyard. He put a hedge around it, dug a wine press, and built a watchtower. Then he rented it to tenant farmers and went away on a journey. When harvest time came, he sent his servants to the tenants to collect his share of the grapes.
The tenants grabbed his servants. They beat one, killed another, and stoned a third. So he sent more servants than before, and the tenants treated them the same way.

Last of all he sent his son. He said, 'They will respect my son.' But when the tenants saw the son, they said to each other, 'This is the heir. Come on, let's kill him and take his inheritance.' So they seized him, threw him out of the vineyard, and killed him.

So when the owner of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants?" They answered, "He will put those wicked men to a terrible end. Then he will rent the vineyard to other tenants who will give him his share at harvest time."

Jesus said to them, "Have you never read this in the Scriptures: 'The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. The Lord has done this, and it is wonderful to see'? So I tell you, the Kingdom of God will be taken from you and given to a people who will produce its fruit."

plain.carry: God has given me everything I need to grow, so this week I will ask what fruit he is looking for in me, and bring my worries to him in prayer.

kids.headline: Good Fruit for God
kids.intro: Today's readings tell stories about a vineyard, a garden where grapes grow. God takes great care of his vineyard, and he hopes it will grow good fruit.
kids.listen: how many times the owner sends people to the vineyard, and who he sends last

Reading 1.box: The prophet Isaiah sings a song about a man who worked very hard on his vineyard, but it grew only sour grapes. The vineyard stands for God's people. The good fruit God wanted was kindness and fairness.

chunks.text: Isaiah sings about his friend's vineyard on a sunny hill. His friend dug the soil, took out all the rocks, and planted the very best vines. He built a tower to watch over it. He hoped for sweet grapes, but only sour wild grapes grew.
The owner asks the people, "You decide. What else could I have done for my vineyard? I did everything. Why did it grow sour grapes?"

"So I will take down its fence and its wall. Animals will come in and trample it. Weeds and thorns will grow, and no rain will fall." Then Isaiah explains: the vineyard is God's people. God hoped they would be fair and good to each other. Instead, the weak were being hurt and people were crying for help.

Responsorial Psalm.box: This song says God's people are like a grapevine God planted and loved. When the vine is hurt, the people ask God to come and take care of it again.

Reading 2.box: Saint Paul wrote this letter to his friends in a city called Philippi. He tells them not to worry, but to talk to God about everything and to fill their minds with good things.

chunks.text: Don't worry about anything. Tell God what you need, and say thank you too. Then God will give you his peace, a peace bigger than you can understand, and it will keep your heart and mind safe with Jesus.
Think about things that are true, good, fair, clean, and lovely. Think about things people can praise. Do the good things you learned and saw me do. Then the God of peace will be with you.

Gospel.box: Jesus tells a story about farmers who were taking care of someone else's vineyard. When the owner sent people to collect the grapes, the farmers hurt them, and in the end they even killed the owner's son. Jesus was talking about himself, because he is God's Son.

chunks.text: Jesus told a story. A man planted a vineyard, put a fence around it, and built a tower. He let some farmers take care of it while he went far away. At harvest time he sent his servants to get his grapes. But the farmers beat one servant, killed another, and threw stones at another.

The owner sent even more servants, and the farmers hurt them too. At last he sent his own son. He said, "They will respect my son." But the farmers said, "This son will get the vineyard someday. Let's kill him and keep it for ourselves." So they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him.

Jesus asked, "What will the owner do now?" The people said, "He will punish those bad farmers and give the vineyard to farmers who will share the grapes." Jesus said, "The Bible says the stone the builders threw away became the most important stone of all. God did this, and it is wonderful. God's Kingdom will be given to people who grow good fruit."

word.meaning: A vineyard is a field or garden where people grow grapes on vines.

kids.draw: Draw a vineyard full of grapes, and on each bunch write one good thing you can do for someone this week.
kids.ask: If God is the gardener and you are part of his vineyard, what good fruit could you grow?

family.opener: Today we will hear two stories about a vineyard, and in both of them the owner does everything he can and then waits to see what grows.
questions: What has God given our family that helps us grow, the way the owner cared for his vineyard?
Why do you think the owner kept sending people, even after the farmers hurt the first ones?
What does good fruit look like in our home, at school, or at work?
family.try: Each evening this week, have everyone name one worry to give to God and one thing to thank him for, as Saint Paul suggests.
family.pray: Loving God, you planted us and care for us every day, so help our family grow good fruit of kindness, fairness, and peace.
